# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

Let me analyze the current state and plan the task.

The goal is to tighten an M8 bolt to 14-18 N·m (aim for ~15.5-16 N·m), then retract the socket more than 30 mm from the head top.

Current state:
- Socket is far away: 84.65 mm short of head top, 231.46 mm off axis, 22.12 deg tilted.
- The bolt head top is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439), axis points along (0, 0.342, 0.940).
- The socket needs to be aimed along the bolt axis. Note: socket z points out of the socket. The bolt axis "points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940)". So the socket's z should point along the bolt axis direction? Wait — the socket's axis points out of the socket (tool z). The bolt axis points out of the head. To seat the socket on the head, the socket's axis should align with the bolt's axis, both pointing out. The head top is at the given position, and the axis points outward from the head. So the socket should be positioned beyond the head top along the axis direction, with socket z pointing along the axis (out of the head). Wait, but the socket needs to go over the head from the outside... Hmm.

Actually, let's think: the bolt head top is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439). The bolt axis points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940). So the bolt extends from the head in the direction (0, 0.342, 0.940). The socket goes over the head from the outside (from the direction opposite to where the bolt extends? No...).

Hmm, actually for a bolt, the head is on one side and the thread extends out the other side. The axis "points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940)" — this is the direction from the head along the bolt shaft. To put a socket over the head, you approach from outside the head... Actually a socket goes over the head from the side where the head is exposed. If the axis points out of the head (along the shaft direction), then the socket approaches from the opposite direction? No wait.

Let me reconsider. The socket's open face is where you put the head in. The socket z points out of the socket (away from the open face? No — "z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket"). Hmm, "Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket." So z points out of the socket, i.e., from the open face outward? That's ambiguous. "The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis." So the socket extends 0.16 m from the flange along its axis.

The readings: "socket's face is 84.65 mm short of the head top" — depth on head is negative, meaning the socket face hasn't reached the head. "socket axis off the bolt axis: 231.46 mm". 

The ready aim to centre on axis where it is now: aim point [0.42000, 0.04394, 0.51855], socket_toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]. Note the head top is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439). The aim point [0.42, 0.04394, 0.51855] is head top + 0.342*0.029 + 0.940*0.029... let's compute: 0.04394 - 0.015 = 0.02894 ≈ 0.342 * 0.0846. 0.51855 - 0.439 = 0.07955 ≈ 0.940 * 0.0846. So the aim point is 84.6 mm beyond the head top along the axis direction (0, 0.342, 0.940). And socket_toward is (0, -0.3419, -0.9397) which is the opposite of the axis direction! So the socket z points opposite to the bolt axis — i.e., the socket points toward the head from beyond it? Hmm wait.

Actually socket_toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397] = -(0, 0.342, 0.940). So the socket z points in the direction opposite to the bolt axis direction. The socket's face (open face) is at the aim point, 84.6 mm beyond the head top (further along the axis from the head). The socket z points back toward the head. So the socket is positioned beyond the head (along shaft direction), facing back toward the head, and will move backward (toward decreasing along-axis) to go over the head.

So "out from the head top" means along the socket's pointing direction (toward the head and past it). The 50 mm out aim: [0.420, 0.03210, 0.48599]. Difference from head top: (0, 0.0171, 0.04699) ≈ 0.05 * (0, 0.342, 0.940) = (0, 0.0171, 0.047). Yes! So 50 mm out means 50 mm beyond the head top along the axis direction (away from where the bolt shaft goes? No — along the axis direction as given). Hmm wait, the axis points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940). The aim point 50 mm out is at head top + 50mm * (0, 0.342, 0.940). So the socket is beyond the head top in the direction the axis points. And socket z points opposite (back toward the head). Then to seat, you push along socket z (negative... push with positive mm moves along socket z direction). Push moves the tool along the socket's pointing direction, which is back toward the head. So pushing moves the socket over the head. Good.

Wait, but actually — which side does the socket approach from? If the bolt axis points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940), that's the direction from the head into the bolt shaft. The socket needs to go over the head. The head is at the top; the socket approaches from the outside. Hmm, physically, if the bolt shaft goes in direction (0, 0.342, 0.940) from the head, the head is like a flange, and you'd put the socket on the head from the side opposite... no, you put a socket on the head from the same side as the head faces. The head's "top" — the bolt head is typically between the socket and the shaft? No. A bolt: head on one end, threads on the other. The socket goes over the head from the head side. The axis "points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940)" might mean the axis direction going out from the head face (the side the socket approaches from). Given the ready computations, the socket is placed beyond the head top along (0, 0.342, 0.940) and faces back toward the head. Then pushing along socket z (which is -(0,0.342,0.940)) moves the socket toward and over the head. That's consistent: socket face at head top + 50mm*axis_dir, facing back; push moves it back to the head top and over it.

OK so the plan:
1. Aim to "put it 50 mm out from the head top on the axis": aim [0.420, 0.03210, 0.48599], toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397].
2. Then centre it 0.5 mm out from head top: aim [0.420, 0.01517, 0.43947], same toward. This is 0.5 mm beyond head top along axis.
3. seat() — closed loop to engage the socket.
4. tighten_to(16) or so — torque 15.5-16.
5. unload()
6. retract(50) — move to 50 mm from head top (>30 mm clears).
7. done.

Also need to handle hex alignment: the socket only goes over a head whose flats line up, repeating every 60 degrees. The seat() function handles unwinding if a corner catches. Also wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from zero.

Current joint 6 position is -0.0497 rad, fine.

Time limit: 30 s total. Each command takes time. Let's be efficient.

First move: aim to 50 mm out. The arm needs to move from current pose to that. That's one command. Then aim to 0.5 mm out (second command). Then seat (third). Then tighten_to (fourth). Then unload (fifth). Then retract (sixth). That's 6 commands. Each command's time counts toward the 30 s limit. Movements: the arm moves within limits; time depends on distance. Probably each aim takes a few seconds. Should be OK within 30 s.

Let me start with the first aim.

aim(aim=[0.420, 0.03210, 0.48599], socket_toward=[0, -0.3419, -0.9397])

The tool turns as little as it can; moves in a straight line. From far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first — the description says "from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head." So calling aim with the 50 mm out point will go there directly. Good.

Let me call aim with the 50 mm out pose.

function.name: turn

function.name: unload

The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. # Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

message.content: Unloaded (drive torque ~0 N·m). Now retracting to 50mm from the head top (well over the 30mm requirement).
message.reasoning_content: Unloaded successfully (drive torque is now ~0 N·m). Now I need to retract the socket to more than 30mm from the head top. The retract function takes a distance in mm of the socket face from the head top. I need more than 30mm, so 50mm is a good choice (as suggested in the instructions).
